title: Does Your Team Agree on Performance Standards?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The Admired Leadership newsletter argues that teams quietly carry different mental models of what good work looks like, and that quality suffers when those definitions diverge. The piece points to research showing that teams with shared mental models coordinate and perform better, yet many teams assume agreement they do not have. The remedy is to translate broad expectations such as "respond quickly" into observable behaviors, then test each one by asking whether it can be observed or measured. Leaders are told to separate genuine standards from personal preferences, because preferences dressed as standards teach people to please the boss. The most durable standards are co-written with the team, starting from examples of exceptional and weak work. The essay closes by tying calibration and commitment together: a standard argued into existence by the team will be defended long after the leader leaves the room.
points: Vague expectations like "fast" or "accountable" hide competing definitions, so each one needs a behavioral translation such as acknowledging client requests within two hours.
The test for a usable standard is simple: if the behavior cannot be observed or measured, it needs more precision.
Leaders must separate performance standards from personal working-style preferences, or the team learns that good performance means pleasing the leader.
A practical way to co-author standards is to have each person bring one exceptional and one weak piece of work, then name exactly what separated them.
Periodic calibration against the shared standard, before pressure arrives, turns compliance into commitment.
quotes: Getting a team on the same page about what constitutes exceptional performance is one of the greatest challenges of leadership across all domains.
The remedy is specific, concrete descriptions of behavior followed by a useful test: If the behavior can’t be observed or measured, it needs more precision.
When preferences masquerade as standards, team members learn that good performance is more about pleasing the leader than it is about doing great work.
Ask each team member to bring one example of work they consider exceptional and one that fell short. Then have the group name exactly what separated them.
Studies of performance evaluation show that raters judge the same work very differently until they are calibrated to a shared standard.
Compliance lasts only as long as someone is watching. Commitment lasts because people believe the standard is right.
